evidence.claim: Coal towns and mining camps linked by Virginia’s winding byways
evidence.quote: This 68-mile loop travels from Norton through the communities of Appalachia, Pennington Gap and Big Stone Gap and travels a few backroads past old and new mining camps.

evidence.claim: winding byways
evidence.quote: Many of the roads are curvy, twisty with just a few hairpin turns .

evidence.claim: Virginia’s Coal Heritage Trail links coalfield towns over a network of roads through seven counties.
evidence.quote: The Virginia Coal Heritage Trail officially begins at the Pocahontas Exhibition Mine in Pocahontas and travels 325 miles through seven counties.

evidence.claim: On the Norton/Wise/Lee loop, back roads pass old and new mining camps, with curves and a few hairpin turns.
evidence.quote: This 68-mile loop travels from Norton through the communities of Appalachia, Pennington Gap and Big Stone Gap and travels a few backroads past old and new mining camps.

evidence.claim: The Heart of Appalachia Tourism Authority presents the trail as a way to experience mining towns’ cultural heritage, including working mines, museums and mountain music halls.
evidence.quote: Experience the cultural heritage of southwestern Virginia’s coal mining towns on over 300 miles of scenic byways. Driving through seven counties, travelers can see a range attractions, working mines, museums, outdoor thrills, and mountain music halls.

evidence.claim: The 157-mile Pocahontas-to-St. Paul section passes more than fifty coal-related sites visible from the road, through Tazewell, Buchanan, Dickenson, Russell and Wise counties.
evidence.quote: A 157-mile historic trail from Pocahontas to St. Paul Virginia through the counties of Tazewell, Buchanan, Dickenson, Russell & Wise starting at the first and largest mining town in the Virginia Coalfields and traveling past over 50 coal-related sites visible from the byway.

evidence.claim: Tazewell
evidence.quote: U.S. Routes 19 and 460 in Tazewell County, 17.43 miles, from Bluefield to Tazewell;

evidence.claim: In 2007, Virginia’s General Assembly designated the highway segments as both the Virginia Coal Heritage Trail and Virginia byways.
evidence.quote: An Act to designate certain highway segments as the "Virginia Coal Heritage Trail" and to designate those highway segments as Virginia byways. [H 3094] Approved March 19, 2007

evidence.claim: Heart of Appalachia developed the trail with counties, planning districts, tourism partners and community groups.
evidence.quote: The Virginia Coal Heritage Trail was developed by collaborative effort of the Heart of Appalachia and the counties we represent

evidence.claim: planning districts, tourism partners and community groups
evidence.quote: along with Lenowisco & Cumberland Plateau Planning Districts, Virginia Tourism Corporation, Dante Lives On, The Crooked Road , our legislators and many other community stakeholders.

evidence.claim: Each county developed its section, and communities divided the journey into three parts with food, fuel and lodging at their ends.
evidence.quote: Each of the counties developed their particular section of the trail. Working with the communities along the route, it was decided to divide the trail into three parts to enable the traveler to begin and end their trips in areas offering amenities such as gas, food and lodging.

evidence.claim: The partnership’s stated mission joins interpretation and promotion with protection and management of the trail through Southwest Virginia’s coalfields.
evidence.quote: The mission is to interpret, protect, promote, and manage the trail system that travels through the coalfields of Southwest Virginia.

evidence.claim: The official starting point is Pocahontas Exhibition Mine.
evidence.quote: The Virginia Coal Heritage Trail officially begins at the Pocahontas Exhibition Mine

evidence.claim: For a journey toward that end, the western loops connect Coeburn and Norton with Big Stone Gap and St. Paul.
evidence.quote: passing through or by the communities of Dungannon, Clinchfield, Duffield, Big Stone Gap, Norton, Tacoma, Coeburn before ending back at St. Paul.

evidence.claim: Continue through the coalfields toward Grundy, then Whitewood, Richlands and Tazewell, reaching Pocahontas by way of Bluefield.
evidence.quote: Virginia Route 102 in Tazewell County and Mercer County, West Virginia, 10.83 miles, from Pocahontas to Bluefield;

evidence.quote: Virginia Route 83 and U.S. Route 460 in Buchanan County, 4.29 miles, from Vansant to Grundy;

evidence.claim: then Whitewood
evidence.quote: Virginia Route 635 in Buchanan County, 7.66 miles, from Virginia Route 621 to Virginia Route 638 at Whitewood;

evidence.claim: Richlands
evidence.quote: Virginia Route 67 in Tazewell County, 7.10 miles, from Richlands to Jewell Ridge;

evidence.claim: Coal and iron development made Big Stone Gap an important center in the 1880s and 1890s.
evidence.quote: The town served as an important center for coal and iron development in the 1880s and 1890s

evidence.claim: Its museums preserve different parts of that story.
evidence.quote: Big Stone Gap is home to several museums.

evidence.claim: The Southwest Virginia Museum occupies a house completed in 1895 and acquired by C. Bascom Slemp in 1929.
evidence.quote: Construction of the building was completed in 1895 and purchased by Slemp in 1929.

evidence.claim: The Southwest Virginia Museum occupies a house
evidence.quote: The Southwest Virginia Museum Historical State Park is located in the downtown area in the former home of C. Bascom Slemp.

evidence.claim: Before his death, Slemp established a foundation and hoped the house would become a museum.
evidence.quote: Before his death in 1943, Slemp established the C. Bascom Slemp Foundation and hoped to see the house turned into a museum.

evidence.claim: Virginia acquired it in 1946, and the foundation donated the initial collection.
evidence.quote: In 1946 the state of Virginia acquired the home, and the Slemp Foundation donated the initial collection from Slemp's personal belongings.

evidence.claim: The town’s Meador Coal Museum draws on objects collected during Meador’s work with the Westmoreland Coal Company.
evidence.quote: Meador, to whom the museum is dedicated, collected many of the objects displayed in the museum from his time with the Westmoreland Coal Company

evidence.claim: Dedicated in 1982 after his death, that museum preserves the collection he assembled during the first half of the twentieth century.
evidence.quote: The museum was dedicated in 1982 after his death.

evidence.claim: during the first half of the twentieth century
evidence.quote: from his time with the Westmoreland Coal Company during the first half of the 20th century.

evidence.claim: Grundy’s flood-control project changed the ground beneath the town.
evidence.quote: A 21st-century project to relocate much of the town to higher ground has been completed.

evidence.claim: After repeated floods of the Levisa Fork, a relocation project began in 2001.
evidence.quote: The project started in 2001.

evidence.claim: After repeated floods of the Levisa Fork
evidence.quote: Since 1929, Grundy has suffered nine major floods of the adjoining Levisa Fork River.

evidence.claim: Workers blasted the mountain across the river to create 13 acres of relatively level land, then installed utilities and built new bridges.
evidence.quote: The mountain on the other side of the Levisa Fork was blasted to create 13 acres (53,000 m2) of relatively level land.  After a few years of blasting, utilities were placed and new bridges were built across the river.

evidence.claim: Buildings backing onto the river were demolished, and a flood wall now protects the county courthouse.
evidence.quote: Buildings backing on the river have been demolished, and a new flood wall protects the county courthouse.

evidence.claim: US 460 was moved to the top of that wall.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 460 was relocated to the top of the flood wall.

evidence.claim: The altered road and riverfront are part of the same effort to move businesses out of flood danger.
evidence.quote: It is notable for having major businesses relocated in the 21st century to higher ground to prevent such damage in the future.

evidence.claim: The courthouse protected by that wall was built in 1905–06, then rebuilt and expanded by 1917 after a fire gutted it in 1915.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1905–06.

evidence.claim: then rebuilt and expanded by 1917 after a fire gutted it in 1915
evidence.quote: A 1915 fire gutted most of the downtown, including the courthouse, which was rebuilt and expanded by 1917.

evidence.claim: Visitors once drove their own cars through Pocahontas Exhibition Mine, entering through the fan opening and leaving through the original mine entry.
evidence.quote: Uniquely, it was possible to drive one's automobile through the mine, entering through the fan opening and exiting through the original entry.

evidence.claim: Opened for mining in 1882, it became the United States’ first exhibition coal mine in 1938.
evidence.quote: opening in 1882. In 1938 it became the first exhibition coal mine in the United States.

evidence.claim: The drive-through practice ended in 1970 because exhaust damaged the mine roof.
evidence.quote: The practice continued until 1970, when it was discontinued due to damage to the roof of the mine from car exhaust.

evidence.claim: The tunnel remains open to tourists beside the former coal office and shower house, now converted into a coal museum.
evidence.quote: the tunnel remains open to tourists alongside the old Coal office and shower house now turned into a coal museum.

evidence.claim: Within a hundred yards of the mine, an old railroad track has become a two-mile walking and bicycle path, another change in how people move through the mining landscape.
evidence.quote: Within 100 yards is the old railroad track now converted into a 2-mile walking and bicycle path.

flags: Moments follow ascending app-strip mileage: Big Stone Gap 36.54, Grundy 168.45, Pocahontas 255.18. The official trail starts at Pocahontas, opposite this orientation. Loops are a network; overview is geographic orientation, not turn-by-turn navigation.

Trail operator gives 325 miles overall, while the three named parts total 311.5 miles (157, 86.5 and 68). Catalog mapped distance is 327.1 miles. Total omitted because coverage difference is unresolved.

Pocahontas coal seam is 12 feet in the trail source and 13 feet in the town source; dimension omitted. Cache lacks current mine tour logistics; do not infer automobile access from the historic drive-through story.
Grundy article says the last major flood was in 1977, then documents a 1984 flood. Repeated flooding and completed relocation retained; exact flood count and final-flood claim omitted.
All three current moments retained with exact titles, at and motifs where supplied. No current substantive claim lacks cache support; Big Stone Gap nickname comparison omitted for focus.
